meaning: A command or invitation used by men toward equals or subordinates. It sounds unhurried and a little lordly. In old prayers it is also used to ask a deity for something.
connection: Verb masu-stem + たまえ (する→したまえ, 来る→来たまえ)

senses.label: Command / invitation
senses.meaning: An order or invitation from a superior to a subordinate, or from an elder to a younger person. It sounds relaxed, dignified and a bit pompous, like “Come now, do ...”. Today you mostly hear it from old-fashioned male characters in novels, manga and dramas.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + たまえ (来たまえ・座りたまえ・食べたまえ)
examples: You there, come over here a moment.
Don't hold back. Eat some more.
Now then, have a seat there.

senses.label: 〜てくれたまえ
senses.meaning: 「〜てくれたまえ」 is a request or instruction from someone higher up. It is a little softer than plain 「〜たまえ」, like “Do this for me”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれたまえ
examples: Have this document finished by tomorrow.
If anything comes up, contact me anytime.

senses.label: Prayer (classical)
senses.meaning: In prayers and ritual texts, 「給え」 keeps its original respectful meaning toward gods and buddhas: “Please, (O god), do ...”. It is usually written with the kanji 「給え」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 給え (守り給え・清め給え)
examples: O God, protect us.
Purify us, cleanse us.

notes: Use it only toward equals or subordinates. It is mostly male speech. Using it to a superior or a customer is very rude.
It is rare in modern speech and sounds old-fashioned and pompous. People sometimes use it as a joke, imitating a stuffy boss.
It attaches to the masu-stem, not the te-form: 「食べたまえ」, not ✕「食べてたまえ」. For a request, say 「〜てくれたまえ」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: In mystery novels, an old detective or professor often speaks to young people with 「〜たまえ」.
daily.example: Now, calm down and listen to what I have to say.

daily.title: Watching anime
daily.description: High-status male characters in anime (a student council president, a rich young heir) often talk this way.
daily.example: Behold my true power.

daily.title: Joking with friends
daily.description: Friends imitate an old-fashioned boss on purpose, for a laugh.
daily.example: Come on, it's my treat today. Drink as much as you like.

work.title: An old-school boss to a subordinate
work.description: In TV dramas or in an older-generation workplace, a male boss gives instructions to his staff.
work.example: I'm leaving this matter to you. Do it properly.

etymology: From 「給へ」, the imperative of the classical honorific auxiliary verb 「給ふ（たまふ）」. Originally it was a respectful command toward the listener's action. In modern times it shifted to a slightly lordly command that men use toward equals or subordinates. Prayers still keep the original respectful meaning.

similar.title: 〜なさい
similar.explanation: 〜なさい is a command from parents to children or teachers to students. Both men and women use it, and it sounds gentle. 〜たまえ is mainly male speech and carries a sense of higher status, so it sounds old-fashioned and pompous.

similar.title: 〜ろ・〜え (imperative form)
similar.explanation: The plain imperative 「来い」「座れ」 is direct and rough, used in emergencies or between men. 〜たまえ is also a command, but it sounds relaxed and dignified, not harsh.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: 〜てください is a polite request you can use with anyone. 〜たまえ only goes from higher to lower; using it upward is seriously rude.

meaning: “If you keep doing this (or stay in this state)”, something bad will happen. Often used for advice or criticism.
connection: Verb te-form + いては (casual: 〜ていちゃ; formal: 〜ていたのでは)

senses.label: Keep this up and it's no good
senses.meaning: If a state or habit continues, it will lead to a negative result: “If you keep ..., (something bad will happen)”. The second half is usually negative. It is common when advising or criticizing someone.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いては + negative result (〜ない・だめだ・困る, etc.)
examples: If you keep playing games like that, your eyesight will get worse.
If you eat out every day, no amount of money will be enough.
If you just stay silent, nothing will get across.

senses.label: 〜ていたのでは
senses.meaning: 「〜ていたのでは」 means the same as 「〜ていては」, but it is more formal and stresses “things can't go on like this”. It often gives the reason why a method must change.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いたのでは／いたんでは
examples: If we keep doing it this way, it will never get finished.
If we wait for a reply, we won't make it in time, so we'll start first.

senses.label: Casual 「〜ていちゃ」
senses.meaning: In speech, 「ていては」 often contracts to 「ていちゃ」. It is common when family or friends give advice.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いちゃ
examples: If you're this angry, we can't even talk.
Lying around all the time is bad for your health.

notes: The second half must be a negative result. A positive one is wrong: ✕「毎日勉強していては、合格できる」.
Compared with 「〜ては」, 「〜ていては」 stresses that the state keeps going on.
「〜ていてはいけない」 (“you must not keep ...”) is a prohibition and belongs with 「〜てはいけない」.

daily.title: A parent warning a child
daily.description: A parent sees their child on the phone all the time and warns that this won't do.
daily.example: If you're always looking at your phone, your studying won't get anywhere, will it?

daily.title: Advice from a friend
daily.description: A friend keeps hesitating, so you urge them to act.
daily.example: If you keep hesitating like that, you'll miss your chance.

work.title: Proposing changes in a meeting
work.description: Pointing out the problem with the current method and suggesting a change.
work.example: If we stick with the old methods, we can't win against the competition.

work.title: A boss advising a subordinate
work.description: A boss tells a subordinate not to just wait for instructions.
work.example: If you just wait for instructions, you won't grow.

etymology: Made of 「いて」 (te-form of the auxiliary 「いる」) + the particle 「は」. 「は」 sets up the first part as a hypothetical condition, and 「ている」 shows a continuing state. Together: “if you stay in this state”.

similar.title: 〜ては・〜では (bad result)
similar.explanation: 〜ては just says “if you do this, something bad happens”. 〜ていては stresses that the state keeps going on. 「食べては太る」 means you gain weight whenever you eat; 「食べてばかりいては太る」 means you'll gain weight if you keep eating like this.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: 〜てばかりいる only describes “doing nothing but ...”. 〜ていては turns that state into a condition and must be followed by a bad result. They are often combined: 「遊んでばかりいては」.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: 〜てはいけない is a prohibition. 〜ていては points out that “this will lead to a bad result”; what follows is a result, not a ban.

meaning: Something is absolutely not allowed by rules, morals or social norms. More formal and solemn than 「〜てはいけない」.
connection: Verb te-form + はならない (〜てはなりません／〜てはならぬ)

senses.label: Prohibition / rules
senses.meaning: A prohibition based on law, regulations or rules: “must not”, “shall not”. It sounds formal and serious and is common in regulations, notices and codes of conduct.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + はならない／はなりません
examples: No one except authorized personnel may enter this room.
Minors must not drink alcohol.
During the exam, you must not talk to the person next to you.

senses.label: Strong warning / conviction
senses.meaning: A strong warning from the speaker based on morals or lessons learned: “must never ...”. It often goes with 「決して」 or 「二度と」 and appears in speeches and editorials.
senses.connection: (決して・二度と) + verb te-form + はならない
examples: We must never forget this tragedy.
We must never repeat the same mistake again.

senses.label: 〜であってはならない
senses.meaning: 「Noun / na-adjective + であってはならない」 means “must not be ...”. It is mostly used to make claims about systems or ideals.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective + であってはならない; 「あってはならない」 = must never happen
examples: Discrimination is something that must not exist.
Education must not be the privilege of a few.

notes: It is stiffer and more solemn than 「〜てはいけない」. Saying it to a specific person in daily life can sound preachy.
「なくてはならない」 means something completely different: “must have, indispensable”. Example: 「水は生活になくてはならない」.
The old-style form 「〜てはならぬ」 often appears in proverbs and lines from novels.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News and editorials often use it when talking about the lessons of war or disasters.
daily.example: We must not let this lesson fade.

daily.title: Reading rules and notices
daily.description: Signs in parks and facilities list what is prohibited.
daily.example: Bonfires are prohibited here.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: Work rules and compliance manuals state what is prohibited.
work.example: Employees must not disclose information obtained in the course of their work to outside parties.

work.title: Speeches
work.description: After an accident, a leader stresses the lesson in a speech.
work.example: An accident like this must never happen again.

etymology: Made of 「te-form + は」 (a hypothetical condition) + 「ならない」. 「ならない」 originally meant “won't work, won't do”, so 「〜てはならない」 is literally “if you do ..., it won't do”, which became a prohibition. 「〜てはいけない」 has the same structure and is the conversational version.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Both express prohibition. 〜てはいけない is conversational and everyday. 〜てはならない is written and solemn, used in laws, speeches and universal moral rules.

similar.title: 〜べきではない
similar.explanation: 〜べきではない means “shouldn't (logically)” and expresses the speaker's opinion or advice. 〜てはならない is a stronger “absolutely not allowed”.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: 〜なければならない means “must do”. 〜てはならない means “must not do”. 「なくてはならない」 also means “must”, so don't mix them up.

similar.title: 〜てならない
similar.explanation: 〜てならない (without は) expresses a strong feeling, “terribly ...”, as in 「心配でならない」. It has nothing to do with prohibition.

meaning: An objective inference based on facts or data: “it is thought that ...”, “it is likely that ...”. Common in reports, papers and the news to avoid a flat assertion.
connection: Plain form (「だ」 can be dropped after nouns / na-adjectives) + と考えられる

senses.label: Objective inference
senses.meaning: A judgment that follows naturally from some evidence: “it is thought that ...”, “it is presumed that ...”. It sounds objective and cautious, not a direct assertion.
senses.connection: Plain form + と考えられる／と考えられます
examples: The cause of the accident is thought to be the driver falling asleep.
These ruins are thought to be about 2,000 years old.
The price increase is thought to be due to soaring raw material costs.

senses.label: Also possible
senses.meaning: 「〜とも考えられる」 means “it could also be that ...”. It offers another possible interpretation.
senses.connection: Plain form + とも考えられる
examples: It's also possible that he is lying.
This result could also be mere coincidence.

senses.label: Hard to believe
senses.meaning: 「〜とは考えられない」 means “it's hard to believe that ...”, “it's unthinkable that ...”. It rules out a possibility.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは考えられない／とは考えられません
examples: I can't believe that someone as earnest as him is the culprit.
It's hard to believe a conclusion can be drawn from this data alone.

notes: The 「られる」 in 「考えられる」 is usually seen as spontaneous (“one naturally comes to think”), so it sounds objective, not dogmatic.
「〜と考えられている」 is a view widely held by society or scholars. 「〜と考えられる」 is usually the speaker's own inference from evidence.
「〜と思われる」 is similar but leans toward subjective impression. 「〜と考えられる」 sounds more like a reasoned judgment.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: When news reports the cause of an accident or incident, they often use this non-committal phrasing.
daily.example: According to the police, the fire is believed to have been caused by a carelessly discarded cigarette.

daily.title: Guessing with a friend
daily.description: Speculating with a friend about the cause of something, in slightly careful wording.
daily.example: The train could have been late because of an accident, too.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: Explaining the conclusion of data analysis in a research report.
work.example: The main cause of the drop in sales is thought to be a competitor's new product launch.

work.title: Academic papers
work.description: Carefully presenting an inference in a paper.
work.example: From the above results, it can be concluded that there is a correlation between the two.

etymology: The 「られる」 form of 「考える」. This 「られる」 is usually considered spontaneous (“one naturally comes to think so”), with a hint of potential (“it can be thought”). That is why it is used for impersonal, objective inferences.

similar.title: 〜と考えられている
similar.explanation: 〜と考えられている means “it is generally believed”, a common view in society or academia. 〜と考えられる is usually the speaker's own inference from evidence at that moment.

similar.title: 〜と言える
similar.explanation: 〜と言える means “it can be said that ...” and sums up or evaluates something. 〜と考えられる focuses on guessing causes or possibilities.

similar.title: 〜に違いない
similar.explanation: 〜に違いない is a subjective assertion that the speaker is very sure of. 〜と考えられる sounds objective and leaves room for doubt.

meaning: 「一 + counter + として〜ない」 means “not a single ...”. It stresses total negation.
connection: (誰・何) 一 + counter + として + 〜ない

senses.label: Not a single person
senses.meaning: 「一人として〜ない」 means “not one person ...”. Adding 「誰」 as in 「誰一人として」 makes the negation even stronger.
senses.connection: (誰) 一人 + として + 〜ない
examples: Not a single person in the class was able to solve that problem.
Not one person opposed his opinion.

senses.label: Not a single thing
senses.meaning: 「一つとして〜ない」 means “not a single thing”. 「何一つとして」 is also common.
senses.connection: (何) 一つ + として + 〜ない
examples: No two snowflakes have the same shape.
Not a single thing he said was true.

senses.label: Not once / not a single day
senses.meaning: 「一日として」, 「一度として」, 「一瞬として」 and similar forms negate time or frequency completely: “not a single day / not once / not for a moment”.
senses.connection: 一日・一度・一瞬, etc. + として + 〜ない
examples: He has never missed a single day of practice.
There wasn't a single day I forgot about her.
He has never once broken a promise.

notes: What comes before 「として」 must be the smallest amount, 「一 + counter」, and it must be followed by a negative.
The 「として」 in 「チームの一人として頑張る」 means “as”. It is not this grammar point.
It sounds more formal and emphatic than 「一人も〜ない」 and is common in writing or formal speech.

daily.title: Talking about an experience
daily.description: Telling a friend that an event was empty and nobody came.
daily.example: I went to all that trouble to prepare, but not a single person came.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's perseverance.
daily.example: My grandfather never took a single day off from working in the fields.

work.title: News reports
work.description: Stressing in a report that nobody was hurt.
work.example: Not a single passenger was injured.

work.title: Product introductions
work.description: Stressing that every product is one of a kind.
work.example: Since they are handmade by craftsmen, no two are alike.

etymology: 「として」 is the particle 「と」 + 「して」 (te-form of 「する」), originally “as, regarded as”. 「一人として」 is roughly “even counting as one person”. Paired with a negative, it says even the smallest amount doesn't exist, which makes a total negation.

similar.title: 〜として〜ない
similar.explanation: These are essentially the same grammar point. This entry organizes the uses by people, things and times. The 〜として〜ない entry also covers the double negative 「〜として〜ないものはない」.

similar.title: Question word + も〜ない
similar.explanation: 「誰も来なかった」 is an ordinary total negation. 「誰一人として来なかった」 stresses “not even one”, and sounds heavier and more formal.

similar.title: 〜たりとも
similar.explanation: 「一日たりとも休まない」 also means “not even one ...”, but 〜たりとも is more formal and stronger, often used for resolutions and prohibitions.

title: 〜ばかり (approximately)
meaning: After a quantity, it means “about, around”. 「少しばかり」 means “just a little”.
connection: Quantity word + ばかり; 少し + ばかり

senses.label: About / around
senses.meaning: After words for amount, length of time, distance or money, it gives a rough figure: “about ...”. It is slightly more formal and old-fashioned than 「くらい」.
senses.connection: Number + counter + ばかり (十分ばかり・一週間ばかり・千円ばかり)
examples: I live about a ten-minute walk from the station.
I took about a week off.
Could you lend me about 1,000 yen?

senses.label: 少しばかり
senses.meaning: 「少しばかり」 means a small amount or degree: “a little, slightly”. When giving a gift, 「少しばかりですが」 is a humble phrase.
senses.connection: 少し + ばかり (+ ですが／の + noun)
examples: It's just a little something, but please accept it.
I'm a little tired today.

notes: It only gives an approximate amount. It can't follow a point in time: ✕「三時ばかり」; say 「三時ごろ」.
「来たばかり」 (just did) and 「遊んでばかり」 (doing nothing but) are different uses, so keep them apart.
In everyday speech, 「くらい／ぐらい」 is more common. 「ばかり」 feels a bit formal, old-fashioned or refined.

daily.title: Borrowing money
daily.description: Asking someone you know to lend you a little money.
daily.example: Sorry, but could you lend me about 2,000 yen?

daily.title: Giving a gift
daily.description: Handing over a small gift on a visit, with a humble phrase.
daily.example: It's just a little something, but please enjoy it together.

work.title: Asking your boss
work.description: Asking your boss to spare a little time.
work.example: Could I have about five minutes of your time?

etymology: 「ばかり」 comes from 「はかり」, the noun form of the verb 「はかる（計る・量る）」 (to measure), meaning “an estimate, a rough amount”. From this came the “about” meaning, and later the meanings “only, nothing but” and “just (done)”.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい
similar.explanation: Both express an approximate amount. 〜くらい is the most common and conversational. 〜ばかり is slightly more formal and less used today.

similar.title: 〜ごろ
similar.explanation: 〜ごろ follows a point in time (三時ごろ). 〜ばかり only follows words for amounts (三時間ばかり).

similar.title: 〜ばかり (nothing but)
similar.explanation: 「ばかり」 after a noun or te-form means “only, nothing but” (甘いものばかり食べる). Only after a quantity does it mean “about”.

title: 〜より (starting point, formal)
meaning: Marks the starting point in time or place, or the source of an action. It is a formal version of 「から」, used in notices, announcements and official documents.

senses.label: Starting time
senses.meaning: Marks when something starts: “from ...”. Used in notices, announcements and formal settings. More formal than 「から」.
senses.connection: Time noun + より (本日より・四月一日より・午後三時より)
examples: The meeting will begin at 3 p.m.
Starting today, our business hours will change.
A new system will take effect from April 1.

senses.label: Starting place
senses.meaning: Marks the place of departure or passage: “from ...”. Common in station announcements and travel directions.
senses.connection: Place noun + より (駅より・空港より・三番線より)
examples: It's a five-minute walk from Tokyo Station.
We will be departing from Narita Airport.

senses.label: Source (person / organization)
senses.meaning: Marks the source of information, items or a speech: “from ...”, “by ...”. Mostly used in formal messages and letters.
senses.connection: Person / organization noun + より
examples: Our president will now give a greeting.
A customer called a little while ago.

notes: It is the formal version of 「から」. In everyday conversation, 「から」 sounds more natural.
The 「より」 in 「AよりBのほうが」 is for comparison (“than”). It is not this use.
Signing a letter with 「母より」 means “from Mom”. This is also the source use.

daily.title: Station announcements
daily.description: An announcement tells you which platform a train leaves from.
daily.example: The rapid train will soon depart from Track 3.

daily.title: Reading a shop notice
daily.description: A notice at the shop entrance announces a change in business hours.
daily.example: From October 1, our regular closing day will change to Wednesday.

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: The chair introduces the next speaker.
work.example: Next, the sales manager will give a report.

work.title: Business emails
work.description: Stating the start time of an event in an email.
work.example: The information session will be held in the head office meeting room from 10 a.m.

etymology: 「より」 is a classical case particle that originally had both meanings, “starting point (from)” and “standard of comparison (than)”. In modern speech 「から」 mostly handles the “from” meaning, so the starting-point 「より」 survives mainly in writing and formal settings.

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 〜から is used in all everyday situations. 〜より is written and formal, common in notices, announcements and business documents.

similar.title: 〜は〜より〜 (comparison)
similar.explanation: Comparative 「より」 means “than”: 「去年より暑い」. Starting-point 「より」 is followed by actions like starting, departing or contacting.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: 「〜により」 shows a cause, means or basis (“due to, by, according to”). It is different from 「より」 marking a starting point.

meaning: Given the circumstances or what came before, a result is only natural: “it's natural that ...”, “no wonder ...”.
connection: Verb / adjective te-form + 当然だ; plain form + のも当然だ／のは当然だ

senses.label: 〜て当然だ
senses.meaning: In that situation, a certain result is to be expected: “it's only natural that ...”, “of course ...”. It often follows a reason clause with 「だから」 or 「〜のだから」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form / い-adjective くて / な-adjective で + 当然だ (当然です)
examples: After practicing that much, it's only natural they won.
It's your first time, so of course you can't do it yet.
If you break a promise, you deserve to get scolded.

senses.label: 〜のも当然だ
senses.meaning: 「〜のも当然だ」 picks up a situation just mentioned and says “given that, it's not surprising”: “no wonder ...”, “it's natural that ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + のも当然だ (+ a preceding reason)
examples: If you work overtime every day, no wonder you're tired.
After preparing that much, it's no surprise it succeeded.

senses.label: 〜のは当然だ
senses.meaning: 「〜のは当然だ」 states a general principle or duty: “it goes without saying that ...”, “it's only right that ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + のは当然だ／のは当然のことだ
examples: It goes without saying that you return what you borrow.
It's only natural to put our customers' safety first.

notes: 「当然」 can be replaced with the more casual 「当たり前」: 「できなくて当たり前だよ」.
「〜のも当然だ」 usually shows understanding of something that already happened. 「〜のは当然だ」 usually states a general rule or duty.
「〜として当然だ」 means “natural as a ...” and follows a noun, so the structure is different: 「親として当然のことだ」.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend failed at something on the first try; you tell them not to worry.
daily.example: Everyone fails at first. That's only natural.

daily.title: Commenting on someone's reaction
daily.description: You hear someone got angry and say you understand.
daily.example: If someone said that to me, I'd be angry too. It's only natural.

work.title: A boss praising a subordinate
work.description: The boss thinks a subordinate's success comes from hard work.
work.example: After all that effort, it's only natural you're being recognized.

work.title: Corporate accountability
work.description: A company states its position at a press conference.
work.example: It is only natural for a company to fulfill its duty of accountability.

etymology: 「当然」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “as it should be”. Combined with a te-form (cause or condition) or the nominalizer 「の」, it forms an evaluative pattern: “(because of ...), ... is only natural”.

similar.title: 〜のも無理はない
similar.explanation: Both mean “no wonder”. 〜のも無理はない is mostly used to sympathize with a negative reaction (anger, disappointment). 〜のも当然だ sounds more objective and certain, and works for both good and bad results.

similar.title: 〜のももっともだ
similar.explanation: 〜のももっともだ focuses on “the other person's thinking or claim makes sense”. 〜のも当然だ focuses on “it's bound to happen, logically”.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: 〜わけだ draws a conclusion from facts: “so that's why”. 〜て当然だ evaluates a result as “only to be expected”.

meaning: Someone's reaction, idea or claim is reasonable: “it makes sense that ...”, “no wonder ...”.
connection: Plain form + のももっともだ; noun + はもっともだ (が)

senses.label: Makes sense / no wonder
senses.meaning: Considering the situation, it makes sense that someone thinks or acts that way: “it's understandable that ...”, “no wonder ...”. The first clause often gives the reason.
senses.connection: Plain form + のも (のは) もっともだ
examples: He was kept waiting for three hours, so no wonder he's angry.
With that much opposition, it's understandable that she's unsure.

senses.label: Concession: fair, but ...
senses.meaning: 「〜はもっともだが」 first admits that the other person's view is reasonable, then raises a different view or a practical problem. It is often used to disagree politely.
senses.connection: Noun / 〜こと + はもっともだが／はもっともですが
examples: What you say makes sense, but we don't have the budget right now.
Your anger is completely understandable, but please calm down.

senses.label: ごもっともです
senses.meaning: 「ごもっともです」 is an honorific phrase that shows full agreement with a superior's or client's opinion: “You're quite right”.
senses.connection: ごもっともです／ごもっともな + noun
examples: What you say is entirely reasonable.
I think your opinion is quite reasonable.

notes: 「もっとも」 has three uses: 「尤も」 (reasonable, this entry), 「最も」 (most), and the sentence-initial conjunction 「もっとも、」 (however).
Repeating 「ごもっともです」 too much can sound like empty agreement. It is common when apologizing or handling complaints.
What is being judged is usually someone's feelings, ideas or claims, not an objective natural outcome.

daily.title: Understanding a friend's frustration
daily.description: A friend complains about being stood up, and you show understanding.
daily.example: If someone canceled on you at the last minute, of course you'd be angry.

daily.title: Talking it over with family
daily.description: You first acknowledge a family member's view, then say what you think.
daily.example: I get why you're worried, Mom, but I'm an adult now, so I'll be fine.

work.title: Handling a customer complaint
work.description: Customer service shows understanding of a customer's dissatisfaction.
work.example: It's completely understandable that you're dissatisfied.

work.title: Disagreeing politely in a meeting
work.description: You first agree with a colleague's point, then point out a problem.
work.example: Your point is well taken, but the schedule makes it difficult.

etymology: 「もっとも」 is written 「尤も」 in kanji and originally meant “reasonable, logical”. It sounds the same as 「最も」 (most) but has a different origin. From “reasonable” it also developed the sentence-initial meaning “however, that said”.

similar.title: 〜のも当然だ
similar.explanation: 〜のも当然だ stresses “it's bound to happen, logically”. 〜のももっともだ focuses on “the other person's thinking or reaction makes sense”, often with understanding or sympathy.

similar.title: 〜のも無理はない
similar.explanation: 〜のも無理はない is mostly used to sympathize with someone's negative feelings or mistakes. 〜のももっともだ leans more toward approving someone's view or claim as reasonable.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: 〜わけだ is the speaker suddenly understanding and drawing a conclusion. 〜のももっともだ approves of someone else's reaction.

meaning: A written form of 「〜ではないだろうか」. It puts forward a guess or claim indirectly: “isn't it perhaps ...?”, “I suspect ...”.
connection: Noun / na-adjective + ではあるまいか; plain form + のではあるまいか

senses.label: Indirect guess / claim
senses.meaning: After a noun or na-adjective, the speaker cautiously puts forward their own judgment: “isn't it ...?”, “perhaps it is ...”. It sounds literary and a bit old-fashioned.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + ではあるまいか
examples: Isn't this, perhaps, his true feeling?
Isn't this plan a little unreasonable?

senses.label: 〜のではあるまいか
senses.meaning: After verbs and adjectives, use 「〜のではあるまいか」 to guess about a situation. Common in commentary, essays and papers.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form + のではあるまいか
examples: Perhaps he won't ever come back.
Isn't there a flaw in the education system behind this problem?

senses.label: Worry / anxiety
senses.meaning: Often used with 「〜と心配する」 or 「〜と不安になる」 to express worry that something bad may happen.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではあるまいかと + 心配する／不安だ／思う
examples: I was terribly anxious that I might fail.
I worried that there might have been an accident.

notes: It is a written, slightly archaic version of 「〜ではないだろうか」 and is almost never used in daily conversation.
「まい」 is a classical auxiliary for negative conjecture. 「あるまい」 ≈ 「ないだろう」.
「〜ではあるまいし」 (“it's not as if ...”) is a different pattern and is not followed by 「か」.

daily.title: Reading essays and commentary
daily.description: In a newspaper column, the writer cautiously offers an opinion.
daily.example: In chasing convenience so hard, aren't we losing something important?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's inner worry.
daily.example: She thought that the letter might never arrive.

work.title: Academic papers
work.description: Carefully putting forward one's own view in a paper.
work.example: Perhaps this phenomenon cannot be explained by conventional theory.

etymology: Made of 「では」 + 「ある」 + the classical negative conjecture auxiliary 「まい」 + the question particle 「か」. 「あるまい」 means “probably isn't”; adding 「か」 turns it into a rhetorical question, “isn't it ...?”, which works as a soft claim: “I suspect it is ...”.

similar.title: 〜のではないか
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning. 〜のではないか (〜んじゃない) is used in conversation and ordinary writing. 〜ではあるまいか is more literary and elegant.

similar.title: 〜ではなかろうか
similar.explanation: Also a written, indirect guess. 〜ではなかろうか uses 「なかろう」 and 〜ではあるまいか uses 「あるまい」; the feel and usage are almost the same.

similar.title: 〜ではあるまいし
similar.explanation: 〜ではあるまいし means “it's not as if ...” and criticizes the listener, followed by advice or a command. It differs from 〜ではあるまいか, which is a guess.

similar.title: 〜まい
similar.explanation: On its own, 〜まい expresses negative conjecture or negative will (“probably not”, “will never”). With 「ではある…か」 it forms a fixed pattern for a soft claim.

meaning: 「一 + counter + として」 paired with a negative means “not a single one, not even once”. It is a strong total negation.
connection: 一 + counter (一人・一つ・一日・一度, etc.) + として + 〜ない

senses.label: Total negation
senses.meaning: It takes the smallest unit, 「一 + counter」, and negates it: “not even one”. It sounds formal and is common in writing or formal speech.
senses.connection: 一 + counter + として + verb nai-form／ない
examples: In these ten years, he has never once complained.
Not a single one of the submitted works was satisfactory.
This past year, there wasn't a single day I could relax.

senses.label: Strengthened with a question word
senses.meaning: Adding 「誰」 or 「何」 gives 「誰一人として」 and 「何一つとして」, which make the negation even stronger: “nobody at all”, “nothing at all”.
senses.connection: 誰一人として／何一つとして + 〜ない
examples: There wasn't a single person I knew at the venue.
I don't remember a single thing about that day.

senses.label: Double negative = all
senses.meaning: 「〜として〜ないものはない」 uses a double negative to mean “there is none that isn't ...”, i.e. “every single one is ...”. It sounds strong and is often used to praise.
senses.connection: 一つ／一人 + として + 〜ないもの (者) はない
examples: Every single dish at this restaurant is delicious.
Every single graduate of this school is thriving in society.

notes: It must be paired with a negative. In affirmative sentences, 「〜として」 means “as”: 「代表の一人として出席する」.
It is more formal and stronger than 「一人も〜ない」 or 「一つも〜ない」.
The double negative 「〜ないものはない」 is easy to misread as negative, but it actually means “all of them are”.

daily.title: Looking back
daily.description: Telling a friend about a habit you kept for years.
daily.example: In my three years of high school, I never missed a single morning practice.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a completely empty street.
daily.example: There wasn't a single human figure to be seen on the midnight street.

work.title: News reports
work.description: A report stresses that no one was hurt in a disaster.
work.example: Not a single resident failed to escape in time.

work.title: Quality assurance
work.description: Assuring a client that every product has been inspected.
work.example: Not a single one of our products has gone uninspected.

etymology: 「として」 is the particle 「と」 + 「して」 (te-form of 「する」), originally “as, regarded as”. 「一つとして」 is roughly “even counting it as just one”. Paired with a negative, it means “not even one”, giving an emphatic total negation.

similar.title: 〜として〜ない（一人として）
similar.explanation: These are essentially the same grammar point. The 〜として〜ない（一人として） entry is organized by people, things and time/frequency. This entry focuses on strengthening with question words and on the double negative.

similar.title: Question word + も〜ない
similar.explanation: 「何も覚えていない」 is an ordinary total negation. 「何一つとして覚えていない」 stresses “not even the slightest bit”, and sounds more formal and heavier.

similar.title: 〜たりとも
similar.explanation: 「一円たりとも無駄にしない」 also means “not even one ...”, but 〜たりとも is stronger and more formal, often used for resolutions and prohibitions.

meaning: “Once it comes to ...”, “when it's a matter of ...”. What follows is the speaker's judgment, guess or resolve.
connection: Noun / plain form + となると／となれば／となったら

senses.label: When it comes to ...
senses.meaning: Brings up a topic or situation and says “once this is involved, things are different”: “when it comes to ...”, “once it's ...”. The second half is usually a judgment or evaluation.
senses.connection: Noun + となると
examples: When it comes to traveling abroad, the preparations are a lot of work.
When it actually comes to getting married, it's hard to make up my mind.
When the talk turns technical, he suddenly comes alive.

senses.label: Hypothetical: if it really ...
senses.meaning: “If this situation actually happens”, followed by a judgment or guess that naturally follows. 「〜となれば」 is more formal and often goes with 「当然」 or 「〜だろう」.
senses.connection: Verb plain form / noun + となると／となれば
examples: If he's coming, everyone will be happy.
If we actually carry out this plan, it will cost quite a lot.

senses.label: Resolve with 「となったら」
senses.meaning: 「〜となったら」 is more casual and often shows resolve: “once it comes to that, I'll ...”. The set phrase 「いざとなったら」 means “if push comes to shove”.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + となったら; いざとなったら
examples: Once I decide to do it, I'll give it everything to the end.
If push comes to shove, I'll take responsibility.

notes: The three forms mean basically the same: 「となると」 is the most common, 「となれば」 is more formal, and 「となったら」 is more casual.
The second half is usually the speaker's judgment, guess, evaluation or resolve, such as “that would be a problem” or “then we'd have to ...”.
「〜ともなると」 (N1) stresses reaching a high level or stage, as in 「社長ともなると忙しい」.

daily.title: Planning a trip with friends
daily.description: A friend suggests going abroad, and you voice a concern.
daily.example: If I'm taking a whole week off, I need to tell my company early.

daily.title: Feelings before a move
daily.description: About to leave a familiar place, you tell your family how you feel.
daily.example: Now that we're actually moving, it's a little sad.

work.title: Evaluating a project
work.description: Discussing the impact of expansion in a meeting.
work.example: If we expand overseas, we'll need to hire local staff.

work.title: News reports
work.description: A report analyzes the impact of a situation.
work.example: If taxes go up, consumer spending could cool down.

etymology: Made of the quoting / result particle 「と」 + the conditional forms of 「なる」: 「なると」, 「なれば」, 「なったら」. Literally “if it becomes ...”, hence “once things reach a certain situation”.

similar.title: 〜とすれば・〜としたら
similar.explanation: 〜とすれば is a pure hypothesis (“supposing ...”) and can be something unlikely. 〜となると usually refers to a situation that has become real or is about to be faced: “when it actually comes to that”.

similar.title: 〜というと
similar.explanation: 〜というと brings up a topic and then makes an association or checks (“speaking of ..., that reminds me of ...”). 〜となると focuses on “once this is involved, things are different”.

similar.title: 〜ともなると・〜ともなれば
similar.explanation: 〜ともなると stresses reaching a high status or degree, as in 「大学生ともなると」. 〜となると just sets up an ordinary situation.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 〜なら is a general condition or suggestion (“if ...”). 〜となると stresses that “things become different”, and is usually followed by a judgment or guess.

title: 〜といったら (introducing a topic)
meaning: Brings up a topic and then names the most typical example: “speaking of ..., it has to be ...”.
connection: Noun + といったら (casual: 〜っていったら)

senses.label: Speaking of ..., it's ...
senses.meaning: Raises a topic, then names the thing people think of first, the most typical example: “when you think of ..., it's ...”. The second half often has an assertive tone with 「やっぱり」 or 「でしょう」.
senses.connection: Noun + といったら (+ やっぱり〜だ)
examples: When you think of summer in Japan, it has to be fireworks festivals.
When you think of Hokkaido, it's crab and ramen.
Speaking of Kyoto specialties, yatsuhashi is famous.

senses.label: Casual 「っていったら」
senses.meaning: In speech it often becomes 「〜っていったら」, used in casual chats with friends.
senses.connection: Noun + っていったら
examples: When it comes to winter food, it's got to be hot pot, right?
What's this town known for?

senses.label: All there is ...
senses.meaning: When the second half has 「くらい」 or 「しか〜ない」, it means “about all there is, is ...”, suggesting there's little worth mentioning.
senses.connection: Noun + といったら + 〜くらいしか〜ない／〜だけだ
examples: As for sights in this town, there's only an old temple.
My hobby? Sleeping, that's about it.

notes: It is almost interchangeable with 「〜といえば」. 「〜といったら」 is more conversational and often carries an assertive tone: “speaking of ..., first and foremost it's this”.
The N3 「〜（こと）といったら」 follows nouns like 「寒さ」 or 「美しさ」 and expresses an extreme degree, often ending in 「〜といったらない」. It is a different use.
「〜と言ったら」 can also simply mean “when (I) said ...”: 「休むと言ったら怒られた」. Tell them apart by context.

daily.title: Telling a foreign friend about Japan
daily.description: Introducing typical things about Japan to a friend from abroad.
daily.example: When you think of spring in Japan, it has to be cherry blossoms.

daily.title: Chatting with friends
daily.description: A friend asks what your hometown is known for.
daily.example: My hometown? All it really has is hot springs.

work.title: Introducing products
work.description: Presenting your company's flagship product to a client.
work.example: When it comes to our flagship products, it's this series.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言ったら」, the conditional of 「言う」. Literally “if (we) speak of ...”. It introduces a topic and brings up the first, most typical thing that comes to mind.

similar.title: 〜といえば
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning, “speaking of ...”. 〜といえば can also be used to follow up on what someone said with an association (「そういえば」). 〜といったら focuses on naming the most typical example and sounds more assertive.

similar.title: 〜（こと）といったら
similar.explanation: The N3 〜といったら follows nouns like 「寒さ」 or 「うれしさ」 to express an extreme degree, often as 「〜といったらない」. This entry is about raising a topic and naming a typical example.

similar.title: 〜というと
similar.explanation: 〜というと can be used to confirm what someone said (「田中さんというと、あの背の高い人？」). 〜といったら is rarely used to confirm.

similar.title: 〜ときたら
similar.explanation: 〜ときたら raises a topic and is usually followed by complaints or criticism (「うちの夫ときたら」). 〜といったら generally names a typical example neutrally.

meaning: Expresses a strong, heartfelt wish: “I'd really love to ...”. Toward others, it means “I really wish (someone) would ...”, and it can also be a soft criticism.
connection: Verb masu-stem + たいものだ; verb te-form + ほしいものだ／もらいたいものだ

senses.label: Strong wish
senses.meaning: A heartfelt, emotional wish from the speaker: “I'd really love to ...”, “I truly hope to ...”. It is more emotional than plain 「〜たい」 and usually refers to long-term wishes that are hard to achieve right away.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + たいものだ／たいものです
examples: Just once, I'd love to see the northern lights.
Someday I'd really like to have my own shop.
When I'm old, I'd love to live a relaxed life in the countryside.

senses.label: Hopes for others
senses.meaning: 「〜てほしいものだ」 expresses how you wish others or a situation would be: “I really wish (someone) would ...”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + ほしいものだ
examples: I really wish young people would read more books.
I truly hope the economy recovers as soon as possible.

senses.label: Soft criticism / request
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらいたいものだ」 and 「〜ないでほしいものだ」 are often used to express dissatisfaction indirectly and ask someone to change: “I really wish you would (not) ...”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらいたいものだ; verb nai-form + でほしいものだ
examples: I really wish you'd finally stop being late to meetings.
I'd like people to listen to others until they finish speaking.
I wish people wouldn't make loud noise in public places.

notes: 「もの」 adds an emotional, exclamatory tone, so it isn't used for small, immediate wishes: ✕「今ジュースを飲みたいものだ」.
The subject is the speaker. It can't express a third person's wish: ✕「彼は留学したいものだ」.
In speech, you'll often hear 「〜たいもんだ」 or 「〜てほしいもんだね」.

daily.title: Talking about dreams
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about what you want to do in the future.
daily.example: Once I retire, I'd love to travel around the world.

daily.title: Reacting to the news
daily.description: Seeing worrying news, you express a hope.
daily.example: I truly hope the world becomes peaceful soon.

work.title: A boss's indirect criticism
work.description: A boss, unhappy with a subordinate's reports, makes a request indirectly.
work.example: At the very least, I'd like you to meet the deadline for your reports.

work.title: Speeches / words of encouragement
work.description: Expressing hopes at a welcome ceremony for new employees.
work.example: I hope all of you will take on challenges without fearing failure.

etymology: Made of the wish forms 「〜たい」 / 「〜てほしい」 + the formal noun 「もの」 + 「だ」. 「ものだ」 originally expresses “the nature of things, common sense” and emotion. Combined with a wish, it gives the wish a deep, heartfelt tone.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: 〜たい is an ordinary wish and works for small, immediate things (水が飲みたい). 〜たいものだ is emotional and usually refers to long-term or hard-to-achieve wishes.

similar.title: 〜てほしい
similar.explanation: 〜てほしい directly states what you want from others. 〜てほしいものだ is more emotional and is often used as a soft criticism.

similar.title: 〜ものだ (common sense / emotion)
similar.explanation: 〜ものだ expresses common sense or emotion (「時間が経つのは早いものだ」). Combined with 「たい」 or 「てほしい」, it specifically expresses a heartfelt wish.

similar.title: 〜ないものか
similar.explanation: 〜ないものか means “isn't there some way to ...?” and expresses an eager hope for something to happen. 〜たいものだ simply voices a wish.

meaning: A polite form of 「時」 or 「際」: “at the time of ...”, “on the occasion of ...”. Mostly used in letters, speeches and other formal settings.
connection: Noun + の / verb dictionary form or ta-form / adjective + 折 (に)

senses.label: On the occasion of ...
senses.meaning: The time when something is done, or an opportunity: “when ...”, “on the occasion of ...”. More polite and refined than 「時」, and mostly used for pleasant or neutral occasions.
senses.connection: Noun + の / verb dictionary form or ta-form + 折に (は)
examples: When I went to Kyoto the other day, I met an old friend.
If you're ever in the area, please do stop by.
Next time I come to Tokyo, I'll visit you to pay my respects.

senses.label: Letter phrase 「折から」
senses.meaning: In seasonal greetings in letters, 「〜折（から）」 means “at this time of ...”. It is usually followed by greetings or wishes for the reader's health.
senses.connection: い-adjective / noun + の + 折 (から), 〜
examples: As the cold is severe, please take good care of yourself.
In this intense summer heat, how is everyone doing?

senses.label: Opportunity (折を見て)
senses.meaning: 「折」 on its own means “opportunity, the right time”. Common phrases: 「折を見て」 (when a chance comes), 「折があれば」 (if there's a chance), 「折に触れて」 (whenever the occasion arises, from time to time).
senses.connection: 折を見て／折があれば／折に触れて
examples: I'll find a good moment to talk to the department manager.
I think of my grandmother's words from time to time.

notes: It is mostly used for pleasant or neutral occasions, not for bad events like accidents or disasters: ✕「事故の折」; say 「事故の際」.
The 「折」 in 「時折」 (sometimes), 「折り紙」 and 「骨折」 has nothing to do with this grammar point.
It is more polite and refined than 「時」 or 「際」, and common in letters, emails and speeches.

daily.title: Writing to a former teacher
daily.description: Writing a letter to a former teacher and ending with wishes for their health.
daily.example: As the seasons change, please take good care of yourself.

daily.title: Making plans with an old friend
daily.description: Promising to meet again when saying goodbye.
daily.example: Next time you come out this way, let me know.

work.title: Business emails
work.description: Inviting a client to drop by when they're in the area.
work.example: If you're ever near our office, please be sure to let us know.

work.title: Speeches
work.description: At a farewell party, looking back on your relationship with someone.
work.example: Thank you very much for your kind hospitality when I visited your company the other day.

etymology: 「折」 is the noun form of the verb 「折る」 (to fold, bend) and originally meant “a fold, a joint”. From “a point in time” it came to mean “time, occasion”. Today it is used as an elegant word for 「時」, mostly in letters and formal settings.

similar.title: 〜際 (に)
similar.explanation: 〜際 is also a formal way to say 「時」, and works for both good and bad events (「事故の際」); it's common in instructions and notices. 〜折 is more refined and mostly used for pleasant or courteous occasions.

similar.title: 〜とき
similar.explanation: 〜とき is the most common and fits any situation. 〜折 is formal and refined, and less common in speech.

similar.title: 〜に際して
similar.explanation: 〜に際して is used for “when starting something special” (入学に際して) and sounds official. 〜折に usually refers to occasions like visits or trips, with a polite, greeting-like tone.
